title: Clay soils, pyrite and the French drain

chapters.title: Introduction
chapters.html:
Some building risks are specific to Québec and the Montréal region: clay soils, pyrite, an aging French drain, buried tanks, vermiculite. Properly identified, they can be managed; ignored, they cost a fortune.

This guide teaches you to spot the warning signs, ask the right questions, and target the right professional checks before you buy.

This content is informational: diagnoses must be made by professionals (inspector, engineer, expert). Each chapter ends with a lined « My notes » page.

chapters.title: Clay soils and foundation movement
chapters.objective: Understand why clay moves and what it implies.
chapters.html:
Understand why clay moves and what it implies.

A large part of the Montréal, Laval and North Shore region sits on clay soils. Clay swells with water and shrinks in dry periods, which can cause foundation movement, cracks and uneven floors — especially during droughts or with large trees nearby that dry out the soil.

  • Warning signs: stair-step cracks, doors/windows that stick, sloping floors.
  • Aggravating factors: mature trees near the foundation, poor drainage, droughts.
  • When in doubt: have it assessed by a professional (sometimes an engineer).
Emilie's tip

Not every crack is serious, but some are. In clay areas, have significant cracks assessed by a pro before buying: it's the difference between a cosmetic detail and a major bill.

chapters.title: Pyrite and pyrrhotite
chapters.objective: Recognize these mineral risks by area.
chapters.html:
Recognize these mineral risks by area.

Pyrite can be present in the backfill under the basement slab in certain areas: as it swells, it lifts and cracks the slab. Pyrrhotite, on the other hand, affects the foundation concrete in certain regions (mostly outside Greater Montréal, but worth knowing) and can degrade it.

  • Pyrite warning signs: heaving and cracking of the basement slab, pressure on partition walls.
  • Verification: a swelling test of the backfill (petrography) by a specialized laboratory.
  • Some areas are more at risk: ask around locally.
Emilie's tip

If a basement slab shows cracking and heaving in an area known for pyrite, insist on a test before buying. The cost of the test is trivial compared to redoing a slab.

chapters.title: The French drain and water management
chapters.objective: Assess the system that keeps the basement dry.
chapters.html:
Assess the system that keeps the basement dry.

The French drain, buried at the base of the foundation, carries water away from the soil. Over time (often a few decades), it can clog or sag, leading to basement infiltration. Replacing it is a costly job (excavation).

  • Warning signs: dampness or infiltration in the basement, efflorescence, odors.
  • Good surface drainage: ground slope and gutters directing water away from the house.
  • A camera can inspect the state of the drain when there's doubt.
Emilie's tip

The age of the French drain is a question to ask systematically on a house over 30 years old. A dry basement today doesn't guarantee a drain in good condition.

chapters.title: Buried tanks, vermiculite and asbestos
chapters.objective: Spot the other Québec points to watch.
chapters.html:
Spot the other Québec points to watch.

  • Buried oil tank (old oil heating): risk of soil contamination and an insurability issue; its presence must be declared and managed.
  • Vermiculite (granular insulation in some older attics/walls): may contain asbestos; have it tested before any work.
  • Other asbestos-containing materials in older buildings: take precautions during renovations.

None of these elements is necessarily a deal-breaker, but each must be identified, assessed and, if needed, costed out before the purchase.

Emilie's tip

These points shouldn't make you flee every old house — they should make you ask questions and target the inspection. A well-understood house is a house you buy with peace of mind.

chapters.title: Action plan
chapters.html:
Your next steps, concretely.

This week

  1. Find out whether the areas I'm targeting are at risk (clay, pyrite).
  2. List the warning signs to watch for during visits.

Within 30 days

  1. Work with the inspector to target the relevant on-site checks.
  2. Plan specialized tests (pyrite, drain, vermiculite) if necessary.

Next

  1. Factor any identified risk into my price and conditions strategy.

chapters.title: Resources & glossary
chapters.html:
• Clay soil: soil that swells and shrinks, potentially moving the foundation.
  • Pyrite: a mineral in the backfill that swells and lifts the basement slab.
  • Pyrrhotite: a mineral that can degrade foundation concrete (certain regions).
  • French drain: a pipe at the base of the foundation that carries away soil water.
  • Vermiculite: old granular insulation that may contain asbestos.
  • Buried tank: an old oil tank, a soil and insurance concern.
